summary: This unit teaches you to lead and manage people: to tell leading from managing and build trust, to choose a leadership style, to motivate using the main theories, to build a team and set direction, to delegate and empower, to develop people, to resolve conflict and treat people fairly, to support wellbeing, and to lead change.

blocks.p: Managers get results through other people. This unit teaches you to lead a team: to set direction, choose a suitable leadership style, motivate, build a team, delegate, develop people, deal with conflict, look after fairness and wellbeing, and lead change. It is for supervisors and managers in Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies who are responsible for the work and the welfare of a team.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it means in practice
rows: Tell leading from managing and build trust by what you do
Match your leadership style to the people, the task and the situation
Use the main theories of motivation to find causes and act
Guide a team through its stages, use people's strengths and set clear goals
Give work and authority fairly and safely, keeping accountability
Find training needs, plan development, induct new staff and prepare successors
Handle conflict and treat people fairly
Resolve disagreements, include everyone and act lawfully and ethically
Care for wellbeing and lead change
Notice stress, manage absence and turnover, and lead a team through change
Use results and honest feedback to improve

blocks.note: There is no single best leadership style. Good leaders understand people, read the situation and change their approach when they need to.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Point
Managing
Leading
rows: Plans, organises, staffs and controls the work
Sets direction, inspires and influences people
How and when will the work be done?
Where are we going and why does it matter?

blocks.p: A supervisor needs both: **leading sets direction and inspires; managing plans, organises and controls**. A manager who only controls gets compliance; one who only inspires may get enthusiasm without results.
Trust is the foundation of leadership. Staff trust a leader who:

ul: **keeps promises** and does what she says;
treats everyone **fairly** and consistently;
is honest, including about bad news;
listens and takes concerns seriously;
gives credit, and takes responsibility when things go wrong;
is competent and prepared.

blocks.note: A manager who tells her team that punctuality matters but arrives late herself teaches them that the rule is not serious. People copy what leaders do, not what they say.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: A manager's legal and ethical duties to the people she leads

ul: Provide a **safe workplace** and safe systems of work, as the occupational safety and health duties of an employer require.
Treat staff **fairly under employment law**: terms, pay, leave, discipline and dismissal.
Avoid discrimination and harassment; protect dignity.
Respect privacy and keep personal information confidential.
Be honest and act with integrity in the use of resources.

blocks.p: The **span of control** is the number of staff who report directly to one manager. A very wide span (for example 14 direct reports across three sites) makes it hard to coach and monitor; a very narrow span wastes management time. The right span depends on the complexity of the work, the skill of the staff and how far apart they are. A manager who is overloaded can appoint team leaders or supervisors to narrow the span.
Ask for honest feedback, look at **team results** (output, quality, absence, turnover, customer feedback) and compare. A leader who does not seek feedback may be the last to know of a problem.

head: Style
How the leader behaves
Strengths
Weaknesses
Suits
rows: Decides alone and expects it to be followed
Staff feel unvalued; little new thinking
Asks for views and decides with the team
Slower; may be unclear who decides
Drift, confusion; no support for the less able
Inspires with a shared vision; develops people
Does not build loyalty or ideas

blocks.p: A fire in the kitchen of a Kingston hotel needs the directive style in the first minutes: clear, firm instructions at once. A team of experienced engineers deciding how to cut machine downtime does better with a participative style, drawing on its know-how. A new employee given no guidance and told to 'sort it out' is receiving laissez-faire leadership, which is unsuitable because the person has little skill yet.
Situational leadership says the leader should match her style to the **readiness** of each person for each task: their skill (competence) and their will (confidence and commitment).

head: Readiness
Style
What the leader does
rows: Low skill, high enthusiasm (a keen newcomer)
Gives clear instructions, closely guides and checks
Some skill, low confidence or commitment
Explains, encourages, invites questions and still gives direction
Good skill, but varying confidence or motivation
Listens, encourages, shares decisions; less instruction
Gives the task and authority; stays available if needed

blocks.note: The same person may need different styles for different tasks. An experienced cashier who is confident at the till may need directing when she starts to use a new system.
blocks.label: Tip

ol: Look at the task: urgent, risky, complex?
Look at the person or team: skill, confidence, experience?
Look at the time and the consequences of error.
Choose, explain your approach and be ready to change.

blocks.p: Motivation is the drive that makes people put effort into work. No manager can motivate someone who does not want to be motivated, but she can remove blocks, create conditions and show what is in it for people.

head: Level (bottom to top)
Examples at work
rows: Pay enough to live, rest breaks, food, water
Job security, safe conditions, safe transport home after late shifts
Friendly team, being part of a group
Growth, using your full potential, meaningful work

blocks.p: People generally look to satisfy lower needs first. Staff who worry about getting home safely after a late shift are concerned with **safety needs**, and a manager who solves this removes a barrier before recognition or growth programmes can work.

head: Hygiene factors
Motivators
rows: Pay, working conditions, job security, company policy, supervision, relationships
Achievement, recognition, responsibility, interesting work, advancement, growth

blocks.p: **Hygiene factors** cause dissatisfaction when absent but, when present, do not by themselves motivate. **Motivators** give satisfaction and drive. A manager must keep hygiene factors fair (pay and conditions) and **add** motivators (responsibility, recognition, variety). When staff have fair pay and good conditions yet seem bored and do the minimum, add motivators.

blocks.h: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y

head: Theory X
Theory Y
rows: People dislike work and avoid it; need to be watched and threatened
People enjoy work, will seek responsibility and use self-control

blocks.p: A manager who believes Theory X controls closely and gets compliance and resentment. One who believes Theory Y gives responsibility and often gets more. Most people respond to the way they are treated.

People work hard when they believe three things: **effort will lead to performance**, **performance will lead to a reward**, and **the reward is something they value**. If any link is weak, motivation falls. A bonus for rooms inspected right the first time will not work if staff believe the inspectors judge unfairly (the effort-to-performance link is broken) or do not value the reward.

People compare their effort and reward with those of others. If they think that a colleague is rewarded more for the same work, motivation falls. Make rewards clear, based on criteria, and open to explanation.

ul: Set clear, achievable goals and give feedback.
Recognise good work, quickly, specifically and publicly where appropriate.
Give responsibility and a say in how the work is done.
Offer learning and a path to promotion.
Keep pay, conditions and safety fair.
Listen, and act on what you hear.
Make the link between effort and reward clear and believable.

blocks.note: In many Jamaican workplaces, a sincere 'well done' from a respected supervisor, paid leave for a family event, or a chance to learn a new skill is valued highly, especially where pay rises are limited.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Stage
What happens
What the leader does
rows: Members meet, are polite and unsure; depend on the leader
Give clear purpose, roles and introductions; set direction
Disagreements about roles, methods, and leadership
Clarify roles, handle conflict openly, keep the team on its goal; do not suppress disagreement
Agreed ways of working; trust and cohesion grow
Encourage shared rules, involve the team, strengthen relationships
The team works well with little direction
Delegate, monitor results, support and develop
The task ends and the team breaks up
Review lessons, thank people, and help them to move on

blocks.p: A new project team that argues about roles and methods in its second week is in the **storming** stage. This is normal; the leader's job is to guide the team through it.
Teams work best when they contain a balance of roles. Belbin described nine roles, including:

A leader who knows the strengths and roles of her staff can **match tasks to strengths and fill gaps**. A team with many idea-people but nobody who finishes tasks needs an implementer or completer-finisher.

flow: Understand the organisation's goals and what they mean for your team
Explain the goal, why it matters and what it means for each person
Agree the team's own goals, with measures
Share the plan, roles and timetable
Check understanding and progress, and adjust

blocks.p: If a distribution manager wants her drivers and loaders to understand the firm's new same-day delivery goal, she should **explain the goal, why it matters and what it means for them** before asking for action.
Write team goals as **SMART** goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Example: 'Process 90% of loan applications within 3 working days by 31 March.'

A team charter is a short agreement on how the team will work. It should cover: purpose and goals; roles; ground rules (time keeping, respect, sharing information); communication routine (huddles, meetings, messaging); how decisions are made; how conflict will be raised and handled; how the team will review itself.

ul: Hold short regular **huddles or team meetings** to share updates, solve problems and keep everyone aligned.
For shift teams, **brief each shift in person and confirm it in writing**.
Use the right channel: face-to-face for sensitive matters, writing for facts and decisions.
Listen more than you speak; check that the message was understood.
Share the 'why'.

blocks.p: The first days shape a new employee's view of the workplace. A good induction on the first day includes: a welcome and introductions to the team; **safety rules** and emergency exits; the job, targets and standards; practical details (pay, hours, leave, rules); a named buddy; and a plan for the first weeks.

**Delegation** is giving a staff member the authority and responsibility to carry out a task on the manager's behalf. It frees the manager's time, develops staff and builds trust. The manager remains **accountable** to senior management for the outcome.

head: Delegate
Keep
rows: Routine tasks that others can do well, such as preparing the weekly staff roster or a regular report
Preparing data, drafts and regular reports, with checking
Tasks that develop a staff member's skills
Tasks needing your authority or judgement alone
Work that others can do faster or better
Staff welfare issues that need you

flow: Choose the task and decide the result wanted
Choose the right person: skill, willingness, capacity
Brief clearly: result, authority, resources, deadline, standards
Agree check-in points and how to report
Give support and training; let go of the details
Review the result, give feedback and recognition

head: Do
Do not
rows: Say what result you want and how you will judge it
Dump a task without explaining it
Give the authority needed to do it
Give the task but keep making the decisions
Take over or keep rewriting the work
Punish the first error and take back the job

blocks.p: If a manager delegates a report and then keeps checking and rewriting it, the staff member feels distrusted and stops trying. If the staff member makes a small mistake, review it calmly, help her see how to put it right and treat it as learning, while the manager remains accountable.

**Empowerment** means giving staff the authority, resources and confidence to make decisions within their own work without asking each time. A resort that lets front desk staff refund up to J$15,000 to unhappy guests without asking a manager is empowering them: it speeds service and shows trust. Set clear limits and train people to use the authority well.

ul: Match tasks to skills, interests and capacity.
Look at the whole workload: if two people are overloaded and three have spare time, review the workload and share tasks by skill and time.
**Rotate less popular tasks fairly** across the team: it reduces resentment and builds wider skills.
Be open about how work is shared and listen to concerns.
Check that nobody is working excessive hours.

blocks.p: A **training needs analysis** finds the gap between the skills the job needs and those the staff have now. Use it before introducing a new booking or accounting system.

flow: Identify the skills the job or the new system requires
Assess what each person can do now (observation, appraisal, tests, questions)
List the gaps, by person and by group
Choose the best way to close each gap
Plan, deliver and record training
Evaluate whether performance improved

head: Method
Description
Best for
rows: One-to-one help from a manager or colleague to improve performance
A more experienced person gives long-term career guidance
Working in another role or alongside another person
A stretch task or temporary promotion

blocks.p: The best lasting result usually comes from **a mix of coaching, real tasks and a short course**, not a course alone.
A development plan for each person lists: the goal; the gap; the activity; resources and time; who supports; the date to review; and how progress will be judged. Review it at least every few months.

ul: Give feedback regularly, not only at appraisal.
Describe specific behaviour and its effect, not the person.
Mention strengths as well as areas to improve.
Agree actions together.

blocks.p: **Succession planning** means identifying and preparing staff who could fill key roles in the future. A manager who names and prepares two staff members who could step into her role if she leaves is succession planning. It protects the business and motivates talented people.

Staff leave because of poor supervision, no recognition, no growth, unfair pay, workload or conditions. Use exit interviews and regular conversations to find out. If most leavers say that their supervisors never noticed their work, **train supervisors to give regular recognition and support**. Do not wait for the exit interview: ask current staff.
Disagreement about ideas, **well managed, can improve decisions**. Conflict that becomes personal, or is ignored, damages the team.

head: Approach
When it is useful
rows: Collaborating: work together to meet both sides' needs
Time is short and the issue is moderate
The issue matters more to the other side, or to keep peace
Trivial issues, or a cooling-off period

flow: Act early; do not wait for it to blow up
Meet each person separately and listen
Bring them together to state the facts and each other's concerns
Agree what happened and what each needs
Agree solutions and how to behave in future
Follow up and check that it holds

blocks.p: When two cooks keep arguing over who uses the main oven first, the head chef should meet them together, hear both views and agree a fair schedule. If two senior people no longer speak after a dispute over credit, begin with private conversations, then bring them together to agree facts, interests and the way they will work together; credit for team success can be shared openly.

ul: Share good shifts, overtime and opportunities by clear rules, not by friendship. Favouritism is unfair and damages morale and trust.
Include everyone: a team member who uses a wheelchair should not be left out of a site visit because the site has steps; plan an accessible visit or another way to take part.
Apply discipline and rules consistently.
Respect differences in age, gender, religion, disability and background.
Know the law on discrimination and harassment and act on complaints.

blocks.p: People work better when they are healthy and supported. Watch for signs of stress: more errors, absence, short temper, withdrawal, long hours. **Offer support before health and work suffer.** For a team that works late every night in a year-end close: review priorities, bring in short-term help and plan breaks.

ul: Talk privately and kindly; ask open questions and listen. Do not diagnose.
Point to help available (counselling, leave, employee assistance, a doctor).
Adjust workload or deadlines where possible.
Keep what you are told confidential, except where there is a risk to safety.

blocks.p: A reliable worker who is suddenly absent on several Mondays needs a **private return-to-work talk to find out why**, not a warning. There may be a family, health or transport reason.

flow: Explain why the change is needed and what will happen
Involve the team in the details that they can influence
Listen to concerns and answer honestly
Train and support people
Start with small steps; recognise early successes
Review and adjust

blocks.p: People resist change because of fear (of losing status, skills or jobs), loss of control, extra work or poor past experience. Explain why, listen to concerns and adjust details. If a respected team member is openly negative, **talk with him privately, hear his concerns and involve him**.

blocks.note: Never announce a change by notice only. People accept change more easily when they understand why, have a say in how, and see their leader doing the same.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: explain the difference between leading and managing, and build trust.
describe a manager's legal and ethical duties and explain span of control.
describe autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire, transformational and transactional styles and choose between them.
use situational leadership to match style to a person's readiness.
explain Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor and expectancy theory and use them to solve motivation problems.
describe Tuckman's stages and what the leader does at each stage.
use team roles to match tasks to strengths and fill gaps.
set clear SMART team goals and agree a team charter.
delegate with the result, authority, deadline and check-in points, and say why accountability stays with me.

lead a team through change and judge my own leadership.

terms: Leadership
Setting direction and influencing people to follow.
Management
Planning, organising and controlling work and resources.
Span of control
The number of staff who report directly to one manager.
Autocratic
A style in which the leader decides alone.
Laissez-faire
A hands-off style in which the team decides with little guidance.
Situational leadership
Matching style to the readiness of the person for the task.
Hygiene factors
Herzberg's factors such as pay and conditions that cause dissatisfaction if absent.
Motivators
Herzberg's factors such as achievement and recognition that satisfy and drive.
Self-actualisation
The top of Maslow's hierarchy: fulfilling one's potential.
Theory X and Theory Y
McGregor's pessimistic and optimistic views of people at work.
Storming
The Tuckman stage of conflict over roles and methods.
Delegation
Giving a person authority and responsibility for a task, while remaining accountable.
Empowerment
Giving staff authority and confidence to decide within their own work.
Training needs analysis (TNA)
Finding the gap between required and actual skills.
Succession planning
Preparing staff to fill key roles in future.
Turnover rate
Leavers as a percentage of average staff.

c1.title: A new head of department at a municipal corporation
c1.text: Sharon Gordon has just been appointed head of the building permits department of a municipal corporation in Spanish Town. She spends most of her time on schedules and reports. She has given a new clerk, Kemar, a complicated task with the words 'sort it out'. A senior officer, Mr Reid, who is skilled but has lost confidence since a mistake last month, is hesitating to take decisions. Sharon offers a day off to any team that clears its backlog within a month.

c2.title: Housekeeping staff at an Ocho Rios hotel
c2.text: The housekeeping department of a hotel in Ocho Rios has 40 staff, and many left last year. Staff say they worry about getting home safely after late shifts. Housekeepers have also learned that staff in the laundry section receive a larger bonus for similar work. A bonus for rooms passed first time by the inspector has not improved results, because staff say the inspectors mark unfairly. In exit interviews, leavers say there was no chance to learn new skills.

c3.title: A new project team at a credit union
c3.text: A credit union in Mandeville has formed a project team of eight from different departments to speed up loan approvals. The team contains many people who produce ideas but nobody who finishes tasks or checks detail. In the early weeks members argued about roles. A month later they agree how to run meetings and trust each other more. The project is due to end in June.

c4.title: An accounts manager delegates
c4.text: Natalie Francis is an accounts manager at a construction firm in Kingston. She has 14 direct reports across three sites and is working late every night. She wants to delegate the monthly supplier reconciliation to Andre, an able junior who has never done it. She also has to handle a confidential disciplinary matter for a staff member and prepare the weekly site cost report. A new accounting system arrives next quarter.

c5.title: A regional office of a public agency
c5.text: Mr Orville Haye manages a regional office of a public agency in St Ann. In a month of 20 working days, his team of 10 lost 9 working days to absence. The agency's targets are an absence rate of no more than 3% and staff turnover of no more than 10%. During the year, 6 people left an average staff of 40. Two senior officers have stopped speaking after a disagreement over who should get credit for a report. One cheerful officer has recently been irritable, late and making errors.

questions.q: Which action by Sharon is an example of leading rather than managing?
o: Drawing up a roster for the next three weeks of the whole department
Checking the daily permit count against the monthly target figure for the team
Explaining why faster permits matter to the parish and how the team helps
Writing the monthly progress report for the council's regular meeting
questions.why: Leading means setting direction and helping people see why the work matters. Rosters, counts and reports are management tasks of planning and control.

questions.q: Sharon told Kemar to 'sort it out' with no guidance. What style is this, and is it suitable?
o: Laissez-faire, and not suitable for a newcomer with little skill yet
Laissez-faire, and suitable because it develops independence in the clerk
Autocratic, and suitable because she made the decision on her own
Participative, and suitable because Kemar will learn by trying out ideas
questions.why: Leaving someone alone to decide is laissez-faire. It suits highly skilled people. A newcomer with little skill needs clear direction and close guidance.

questions.q: Mr Reid is skilled but has lost confidence after a mistake. In situational leadership, which approach suits him best?
o: Directing: give him detailed step-by-step instructions to follow
Delegating: leave him alone for a time to recover his confidence
Autocratic: tell him that he must stop hesitating and decide
Supporting: listen, encourage and share decisions with him
questions.why: A skilled person with low confidence needs encouragement and a share in decisions, not detailed instruction or being left alone.

questions.q: Sharon offers a day off to any team that clears its backlog within a month. Which leadership style is this?
o: Transformational: a vision that inspires staff to follow
Transactional: a reward given in exchange for a result
Laissez-faire: no guidance of any kind for the teams
Autocratic: orders issued without any discussion with staff
questions.why: A transactional leader exchanges rewards for performance. A transformational leader inspires through a shared vision and develops people.

questions.q: Staff worry about getting home safely after late shifts. Which of Maslow's needs is most directly affected?
o: Belonging needs
Safety needs
Esteem needs
Self-actualisation
questions.why: Concern for personal safety is a safety need. Maslow suggests that unmet lower needs make it hard for staff to respond to higher-level motivators.

questions.q: The first-time bonus has not improved results because staff think the inspectors mark unfairly. According to expectancy theory, what is the problem?
o: The bonus is so large that it makes the housekeeping staff feel anxious
The staff do not need extra money in order to work as well as they can
The inspectors take far too long to complete their inspections of rooms
Staff do not see that their effort leads to the result that earns the bonus
questions.why: People work hard when they believe effort leads to performance, performance to a reward, and that they value the reward. Unfair marking breaks the first link.

questions.q: Housekeepers learn that staff in the laundry section get a larger bonus for similar work. Which idea best explains the fall in their motivation?
o: Equity: people compare their reward for effort with that of others
Hygiene factors: pay only prevents dissatisfaction, never motivates
Theory X: people dislike work and need to be watched and threatened
Succession planning: staff want to be promoted into other roles
questions.why: People judge fairness by comparing their effort and reward with others'. A perceived unfair difference lowers motivation even when the pay is acceptable.

questions.q: Leavers say there was no chance to learn new skills. What is the best action for retention?
o: Raise the starting pay for all of the new staff who join
Hold a staff party at the end of the year for everyone
Create cross-training and a visible path to supervisor
Stop recording the reasons why staff give for leaving
questions.why: The exit interviews show that growth is missing. Cross-training and a promotion path address the cause, while the other actions miss it.

questions.q: A month later the team agrees how to run meetings and trusts each other more. Which stage of Tuckman's model is this?
o: Forming
Storming
Norming
Adjourning
questions.why: In the norming stage, members agree ways of working and trust grows. Forming is the polite start, storming is the conflict and adjourning is the end.

questions.q: The team has many people with ideas but nobody who finishes tasks. Which team roles does it most need?
o: An implementer or a completer-finisher
A second plant, to add yet more ideas to the team
Another shaper, to push the whole group harder
A resource investigator to find more outside contacts
questions.why: A team needs a balance of roles. Implementers and completer-finishers turn ideas into plans and finish the detail.

questions.q: In June the project ends. What should the leader do in the adjourning stage?
o: Start a new project at once to keep the whole team together
Say nothing at all and let the members drift apart on their own
Blame those who were responsible for the delays in the project
Review what was learned, thank members and help them move on
questions.why: At the end of a team's life, the leader reviews lessons, recognises effort and helps people move on to new roles. This builds goodwill for future teams.

questions.q: What is the best way to set the team's ground rules?
o: The leader writes the rules alone and posts them for the team to follow
Agree them together in a short team charter
Leave the rules until a problem has arisen between some members
Copy the rules of another department in the credit union as they are
questions.why: Rules agreed by the team are owned by the team. A charter covering how meetings run, how decisions are made and how conflict is handled prevents many problems.

questions.q: Which task should Natalie keep, rather than delegate?
o: The weekly site cost report for the directors
The confidential disciplinary matter for a staff member
The monthly supplier reconciliation, once Andre has been briefed
Collecting receipts from the three sites for the month
questions.why: Confidential disciplinary matters need the manager's authority and judgement. Routine reports and reconciliations can be delegated, with checking.

questions.q: Andre makes a small error in his first reconciliation. What is the best response?
o: Take the task back and do it herself in all future months
Warn him in writing about the error in the reconciliation he made
Say nothing, and correct it without telling him about the mistake
Review it calmly, show him the fix and treat it as learning
questions.why: Early mistakes are part of learning. A calm review keeps trust and builds skill, and Natalie remains accountable for the result.

questions.q: Natalie has 14 direct reports across three sites. What is the best action?
o: Appoint site team leaders to narrow her span of control
Visit each of the three sites every day of the week
Stop reviewing any of the work done by the staff
Hold one monthly meeting for all of the 14 staff
questions.why: A very wide span of control makes coaching and monitoring hard. Team leaders reduce the number reporting directly to her and give staff closer support.

questions.q: A new accounting system arrives next quarter. What is the first step of a training needs analysis?
o: Send all of the staff on a two-day course straight away without delay
Wait for the staff to come and ask her for help in their own time
Identify what the system needs and compare it with staff skills now
Choose the trainer and the dates for the classroom sessions first
questions.why: A training needs analysis first finds the gap between the skills needed and the skills present, so that training is targeted.

questions.q: The target absence rate is 3%. The team has 10 staff, each with 20 working days in the month. What is the most working days the team can lose and still meet the target?
o: 3 days
30 days
6 days
60 days
questions.why: Total available days = 10 × 20 = 200. 3% of 200 = 6 days. The team lost 9, which is above the target.

questions.q: With an average of 40 staff and a turnover target of no more than 10%, six people left. What is the correct conclusion?
o: The turnover is 15%, above the target, so find out why
The turnover is 6%, which is below the target of 10% for the year
The turnover is 10%, exactly on target for the whole of the year
Turnover cannot be calculated without knowing why they left the agency
questions.why: 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = 15%, above the 10% target. The next step is to find out why people left, through exit interviews and talking to current staff.

questions.q: Two senior officers have stopped speaking after a dispute over credit for a report. What should Mr Haye do first?
o: Move one of them to another office at once so that they stay apart
Ignore it until the next appraisal discussions are held with each of them
Announce at a staff meeting that credit is shared and say no more of it
Meet each privately, then bring them together to agree facts and ways to work
questions.why: Early action, listening separately and then a facilitated joint conversation, solves the real issue. Ignoring or moving people treats the symptom.

questions.q: An officer who is usually cheerful has become irritable, late and error-prone. What should Mr Haye do first?
o: Give her a written warning for her lateness during this month
Talk to her privately and kindly, ask how she is and point to support
Tell the team to cover for her without saying anything at all to her
Tell her to leave her personal problems at home when she comes to work
questions.why: Changes in behaviour may signal stress. A private, supportive talk, without diagnosing, lets him offer help before her health and work suffer.
